{{Short description|Ordering obtained by a single shuffle}}
In the mathematics of [[permutation]]s and the study of [[shuffling]] [[playing card]]s, a '''riffle shuffle permutation''' is a permutation of a set of <math>n</math> ordered items that can be obtained by a single [[shuffling#Riffle|riffle shuffle]], in which a sorted deck of <math>n</math> cards (increasing top-to-bottom) is cut into two packets and then the two packets are interleaved (e.g. by moving cards one at a time from the bottom of one or the other of the packets to the top of the sorted deck). As a special case of this, a '''<math>(p,q)</math>-shuffle''', for numbers <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> with <math>p+q=n</math>, is a riffle in which the first packet has <math>p</math> cards and the second packet has <math>q</math> cards.<ref name="Weibel">[[Charles Weibel|Weibel, Charles]] (1994). ''An Introduction to Homological Algebra'', p. 181. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref>

Considering a permutation as a bijective function <math>\pi</math> from the set <math>\{1,2,\ldots,n\}</math> to itself, a riffle shuffle is defined as containing only 1 or 2 maximal rising sequences, meaning <math>\{1,2,\ldots,n\}</math> can be decomposed into two disjoint subsets <math>\{i_1<\cdots<i_p\}</math> and <math>\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}</math> with <blockquote><math>\pi(i_1)<\pi(i_2)<\cdots<\pi(i_p)</math>  and  <math>\pi(j_1)<\pi(j_2)<\cdots<\pi(j_q)</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Aldous | first1 = David | author1-link = David Aldous
 | last2 = Diaconis | first2 = Persi | author2-link = Persi Diaconis
 | doi = 10.2307/2323590
 | issue = 5
 | journal = [[The American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | jstor = 2323590
 | mr = 841111
 | pages = 333–348
 | title = Shuffling cards and stopping times
 | url = https://statweb.stanford.edu/~cgates/PERSI/papers/aldous86.pdf
 | volume = 93
 | year = 1986}}</ref> </blockquote>
A permutation with only 1 maximal rising sequence is the identity permutation.

The [[Permutation#Composition of permutations|inverse permutation]] <math>\tau=\pi^{-1}</math>of a riffle shuffle is known as '''Grassmannian permutation''', defined by<blockquote><math>\tau(1)<\ldots<\tau(p) \ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \tau(p+1)<\ldots<\tau(p+q),</math></blockquote>having one [[Permutation#Ascents, descents, runs, exceedances, records|descent]] <math>\tau(p)>\tau(p+1)</math>, or zero descents if <math>\tau</math> is the identity. In [[Schubert calculus]], these index [[Schubert variety|Schubert varieties]] in a Grassmannian space. 

A permutation <math>\pi</math> which is both a riffle shuffle and Grassmannian (i.e. both <math>\pi</math> and its inverse are Grassmannian, or equivalently both are riffle shuffles), is called '''bigrassmannian''' or an '''invertible shuffle'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lascoux |first1=Alain |last2=Schützenberger |first2=Marcel-Paul |date=1996-02-01 |title=Treillis et bases des groupes de Coxeter |journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |volume=3 |issue=2 |article-number=R27 |doi=10.37236/1285 |issn=1077-8926}}</ref>

==Combinatorial enumeration==
Since a <math>(p,q)</math>-shuffle is completely determined by how its first <math>p</math> elements are mapped, the number of <math>(p,q)</math>-shuffles is
<math display=block>\binom{p+q}{p}.</math>

However, the number of distinct riffles is not quite the sum of this formula over all choices of <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> adding to <math>n</math> (which would be <math>2^n</math>), because the [[identity permutation]] can be represented in multiple ways as a <math>(p,q)</math>-shuffle for different values of <math>p</math> and <math>q</math>.
Instead, the number of distinct riffle shuffle permutations of a deck of <math>n</math> cards, for <math>n=1,2,3,\dots</math>, is
{{bi|left=1.6|1, 2, 5, 12, 27, 58, 121, 248, 503, 1014, ... {{OEIS|id=A000325}}}}
More generally, the formula for this number is <math>2^n-n</math>; for instance, there are 4503599627370444 riffle shuffle permutations of a 52-card deck.

The number of bigrassmannian permutations is<ref name="a99">{{citation
 | last = Atkinson | first = M. D. | author-link = Michael D. Atkinson
 | doi = 10.1016/S0012-365X(98)00162-9
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = Discrete Mathematics
 | mr = 1663866
 | pages = 27–38
 | title = Restricted permutations
 | volume = 195
 | year = 1999| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>
<math display=block>\binom{n+1}{3}+1.</math>
For <math>n=1,2,3,\dots</math>, this is
{{bi|left=1.6|1, 2, 5, 11, 21, 36, 57, 85, 121, 166, 221, ... {{OEIS|id=A050407}}}}
and for <math>n=52</math> there are exactly 23427 bigrassmannian shuffles.

==Random distribution==
The [[Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds model]] describes a random [[probability distribution]] on riffle shuffles that is a good match for observed human shuffles.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Diaconis | first = Persi | author-link = Persi Diaconis
 | isbn = 0-940600-14-5
 | location = Hayward, CA
 | mr = 964069
 | publisher = Institute of Mathematical Statistics
 | series = Institute of Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes—Monograph Series, 11
 | title = Group representations in probability and statistics
 | year = 1988}}.</ref> In this model, the [[identity permutation]] has probability <math>(n+1)/2^n</math> of being generated, and all other riffle permutations have equal probability <math>1/2^n</math> of being generated. Based on their analysis of this model, mathematicians have recommended that a deck of 52 cards be given seven riffles in order to thoroughly randomize it.<ref>{{citation|title=In Shuffling Cards, 7 Is Winning Number|first=Gina|last=Kolata|author-link=Gina Kolata|journal=[[New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/01/09/science/in-shuffling-cards-7-is-winning-number.html|date=January 9, 1990}}.</ref>

==Permutation patterns==
A [[permutation pattern|pattern]] in a permutation is a smaller permutation formed from a subsequence of some <math>k</math> values in the permutation by reducing these values to the range from 1 to <math>k</math> while preserving their order. Several important families of permutations can be characterized by a finite set of forbidden patterns, and this is true also of the riffle shuffle permutations: they are exactly the permutations that do not have 321, 2143, and 2413 as patterns.<ref name="a99"/> Thus, for instance, they are a subclass of the [[vexillary permutation]]s, which have 2143 as their only minimal forbidden pattern.<ref>{{citation|title=Permutation patterns, continued fractions, and a group determined by an ordered set|citeseerx = 10.1.1.103.2001|first=Anders|last=Claesson|series=Ph.D. thesis|publisher=Department of Mathematics, Chalmers University of Technology|year=2004}}.</ref>

==Perfect shuffles==
{{main|Faro shuffle}}
A ''perfect shuffle'' is a riffle in which the deck is split into two equal-sized packets, and in which the interleaving between these two packets strictly alternates between the two. There are two types of perfect shuffle, an [[in shuffle]] and an [[out shuffle]], both of which can be performed consistently by some well-trained people. When a deck is repeatedly shuffled using these permutations, it remains much less random than with typical riffle shuffles, and it will return to its initial state after only a small number of perfect shuffles. In particular, a deck of 52 playing cards will be returned to its original ordering after 52 in shuffles or 8 out shuffles. This fact forms the basis of several magic tricks.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Diaconis | first1 = Persi | author1-link = Persi Diaconis
 | last2 = Graham | first2 = R. L. | author2-link = Ronald Graham
 | last3 = Kantor | first3 = William M. |author3-link=William Kantor
 | doi = 10.1016/0196-8858(83)90009-X
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Advances in Applied Mathematics
 | mr = 700845
 | pages = 175–196
 | title = The mathematics of perfect shuffles
 | volume = 4
 | year = 1983}}.</ref>

==Algebra==
Riffle shuffles may be used to define the [[shuffle algebra]]. This is a [[Hopf algebra]] where the basis is a set of words,
and the product is the shuffle product denoted by the sha symbol ш, the sum of all riffle shuffles of two words.

In [[exterior algebra]], the wedge product of a <math>p</math>-form and a <math>q</math>-form can be defined as a sum over <math>(p,q)</math>-shuffles.<ref name=Weibel/>
